Maiden
MAY-den
n. and adj.
From Saxon maegden, a young unmarried woman. Webster 1828: an unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known man; a virgin. Scripture uses it of a girl watching her mistress’s hand, of a dead child raised, and of those spared nothing in a sacked city.

Biblical Definition

Maiden in Scripture is a young unmarried woman or girl, and the word appears at points of great tenderness and great horror. The psalm of ascents makes her posture the picture of the believer’s waiting: as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us (Psalm 123:2). A servant watched her mistress’s hand, not her face, because instruction came by gesture — a fixed, patient attention for the smallest sign, and the psalm makes it the model of prayer. Luke uses the word for Jairus’s daughter at the moment of the miracle: he suffered no man to go in, save Peter, and James, and John, and the father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51), and the Lord took her by the hand and said Maid, arise. And the chronicler uses it in the bleakest sentence of the exile, listing those the Chaldeans spared nothing: had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age (2 Chronicles 36:17). The Lord also names maidens among the servants an unfaithful steward begins to beat when he thinks his master delays (Luke 12:45).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MAIDEN as an unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known a man; a virgin; and as an adjective, pertaining to a virgin, and hence fresh, new, or unused.

expand to see more

MAIDEN, n. — An unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known a man; a virgin.

A female servant; a girl in domestic service.

MAIDEN, a. — Pertaining to a virgin; consisting of virgins; as, a maiden troop.

Fresh; new; unused; as, maiden soil, or a maiden sword — that which has not yet been employed.

From Saxon maegden, a maid — the root also of maid and maidenhood.

Key Scripture

Psalm 123:2 — "Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us."

Luke 8:51 — "And when he came into the house, he suffered no man to go in, save Peter, and James, and John, and the father and the mother of the maiden."

2 Chronicles 36:17 — "Therefore he brought upon them the king of the Chaldees, who slew their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age: he gave them all into his hand."

Luke 12:45 — "But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken;"

Modern Corruption

Psalm 123:2 makes a servant girl’s watching of her mistress’s hand the model of prayer, which is a posture of dependence the modern emphasis on prayer as conversation between equals has largely lost.

expand to see more

The image is precise. A maidservant did not watch her mistress’s face for a mood; she watched the hand, because direction came by gesture and she must not miss it. The psalmist applies this exactly: so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us. Two things follow. The first is attentiveness — the fixed watching of one who has no other resource. The second is patience without a stated term: until. The psalm is short, and its last two verses say the soul is exceedingly filled with the contempt of the proud, so this is not the prayer of the comfortable. Modern devotional language, which encourages the believer to approach God as a friend and to be at ease, has real warrant in John 15:15, but it is not the whole of the Bible’s teaching on prayer, and Psalm 123 is what it has mislaid.

2 Chronicles 36:17 must not be softened, and the dictionary does not attempt it. The Chaldeans had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age, and the chronicler says outright that God brought upon them the king of the Chaldees. The verses before give the reason: the people mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and misused His prophets, until there was no remedy. This is not a text that permits any comfortable reading of God’s patience, and it stands as the historical demonstration of Hebrews 10:31. Luke 8:51 is set here deliberately as its counterweight: the same God who let Jerusalem fall took a dead girl by the hand and called her back.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew almah (H5959), a young woman of marriageable age; naarah (H5291), a girl, a damsel; bethulah (H1330), a virgin; Greek pais (G3816), a girl or boy.

expand to see more

Hebrew naarah (H5291) — a girl, a damsel, a maidservant; the ordinary word for a young woman in service.

Hebrew almah (H5959) — a young woman of marriageable age; the word of Isaiah 7:14, rendered virgin and so quoted in Matthew 1:23.

Hebrew bethulah (H1330) — a virgin; the strict term, used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:16.

Greek pais (G3816) — a child, boy or girl; the father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51).

Greek paidiske (G3814) — a young female servant; the maidens of Luke 12:45.

Usage

"As the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress (Psalm 123:2) — watching a hand, not a face, for the least sign."

"The father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51) — the room emptied before a dead girl was raised."

"Had no compassion upon young man or maiden (2 Chronicles 36:17) — the fall of Jerusalem, stated without softening."
